title: Redwood Private VPC - security architecture deep dive with Crestfield Bank
summary: Deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC) security architecture. Covered network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, peering vs PrivateLink, customer-managed KMS, audit logs/retention, SOC 2 artifacts, RBAC/SSO, and integration with Crestfield SIEM. Agreed next steps: share detailed network diagram, SOC 2 report, and schedule a lab test in a dedicated VPC. Action items assigned.
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC 2 report and security whitepaper (Maya)
Share detailed Private VPC network diagram and proposed route tables (Daniel)
Schedule 2-hour POC lab in Crestfield dev account w/ dedicated VPC (Marcus & Daniel)
Provide pricing/estimates for Dedicated capacity if needed (Maya)
Customer to confirm compliance timeline and required retention windows (Ellen)
action_items: Maya Torres - send SOC 2 report + security whitepaper by 2026-03-27
Daniel Kim - draft VPC diagram + sample route tables by 2026-03-29
Marcus Chen - open dev account for POC and share access details by 2026-03-30
Priya Rao - provide list of mandatory controls (KMS/HSM, retention) by 2026-03-28
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Torres from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Daniel Kim, our solutions SE, and Rina on solutions. Today is mostly a deep dive into the Private / VPC security arch for Crestfield.
[00:00:14] Alex: Hi, Alex Li here, CTO at Crestfield. Priya, Marcus and Ellen are with me. We've got about an hour, maybe a bit more, thanks.
[00:00:22] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: network isolation, ingress/egress, KMS/encryption, audit logs, SSO/RBAC, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:00:35] Priya: Sounds good. We are under a hard compliance window; we need SOC 2 Type II evidence and ensure all egress is controlled.
[00:00:42] Daniel: Understood. We'll show how Redwood Private runs in your VPC, what we control vs what you control, and the standard patterns for restricting ingress and egress.
[00:00:55] Marcus: Quick note - we prefer private connectivity, no internet-facing endpoints if possible. Also want to avoid our data touching third-party networks.
[00:01:02] Daniel: Yep. For the private deployment we support customer-managed VPC where the control plane runs in your network or a customer-managed control plane with private endpoints. To be explicit: no public internet-facing API endpoint unless you opt-in.
[00:01:18] Maya: I'll jump in - typical patterns are: private load balancer + internal NLB, TLS termination in your VPC, and an egress proxy or NAT controlled by you. This lets you enforce egress rules and outbound logging.
[00:01:34] Alex: When you say internal NLB, does Redwood require any inbound rules from outside? How do we handle developer access?
[00:01:41] Daniel: Good question. There are two options: 1) Bastion/jump host + port forwarding, 2) SSM / session manager, or 3) a small, tightly scoped public management endpoint that uses mTLS and IP allowlist. For production we recommend SSM or internal bastion in your management VPC.
[00:02:02] Priya: How about peering vs PrivateLink? We have policies disallowing VPC peering with vendor accounts in some envs.
[00:02:10] Daniel: We support both. If peering is disallowed, PrivateLink (AWS VPC Endpoint Services) is the recommended path - it's single-tenant and traffic stays on the AWS network. We also support Transit Gateway in larger environments. We'll include examples in the diagram.
[00:02:27] Marcus: Does PrivateLink add any limits to throughput or add latency?
[00:02:31] Daniel: Slight overhead but minimal for most workloads. For high-throughput (batch inference), we can recommend Dedicated capacity in the same region or colocated with your workload to avoid cross-VPC hops.
[00:02:45] Ellen: About egress - we need to block any unexpected egress to S3 endpoints outside our account, non-approved APIs, and force all outbound through our proxy for DLP. Can Redwood's runtime respect that?
[00:02:58] Daniel: Yes. In the Private deployment model the inference nodes live in your subnets. Egress passes through your NAT / egress proxy. You get full control of route tables, security groups and NACLs.
[00:03:10] Maya: To add, we can provide a small init container that calls home for health only over mTLS to an internal endpoint you host, or alternatively you can host the control plane yourself.
[00:03:21] Priya: Key management: do you require Redwood-managed KMS or can we use CMK with HSM?
[00:03:28] Daniel: You can use customer-managed keys (CMKs). We integrate with KMS and can be configured to use a customer-owned CMK in AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or an HSM-backed key. The runtime encrypts disk at rest with LUKS or cloud provider disk encryption, and encryption-in-transit uses TLS 1.3 between components.
[00:03:47] Alex: Are keys ever exported to Redwood's control plane?
[00:03:50] Daniel: No. With customer-managed KMS we never receive key material. We request decrypt/encrypt operations via APIs (Decrypt/Encrypt) and you control the IAM policy and key grants. If you want extra isolation we support a bring-your-own-HSM pattern where key operations stay in your HSM.
[00:04:05] Marcus: Audit logs - we need full request/response logging metadata, but sensitive payloads must be redacted. What's Redwood's approach?
[00:04:13] Maya: We provide configurable audit logging. In Private, logs are pushed to your logging endpoint (CloudWatch, Splunk, Elastic, or syslog). By default we capture metadata: request id, model, latency, token counts. Payload capture is configurable and can be disabled; we can also redact or hash prompts.
[00:04:31] Priya: Retention windows - we have to keep metadata logs for 7 years for audits in some lines of business. Can you support that?
[00:04:39] Daniel: Log retention is controlled by your storage. Redwood streams events to your account and you set the retention policies. For compliance that long, you'd configure lifecycle policies in your logging storage. We'll include recommended retention configs in the doc.
[00:04:53] Alex: For SOC 2 evidence, we need controls mapping and system descriptions. Do you have a SOC 2 Type II report and an ISO attestation?
[00:05:01] Maya: Yes - Redwood has SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 attestations for our hosted service. For Private deployments we provide the control mappings and our SOC artifacts; however some controls are customer responsibility once running in your VPC. We'll share the SOC2 and the shared-responsibility matrix.
[00:05:18] Ellen: Excellent. Also we need SSO/SAML + SCIM provisioning and RBAC - how granular is the RBAC?
[00:05:25] Daniel: RBAC is role-based with admin, dev, observer roles out of the box. For Private we can integrate with your SAML IdP for SSO and SCIM for provisioning groups. You can map groups to roles. If you need attribute-based access controls for specific model routes, we can add custom role mappings.
[00:05:44] Priya: What about audit trails for admin actions - user creation, key rotation, config changes - is that captured?
[00:05:50] Daniel: Yes. All control plane events (user changes, role assignments, config rollouts) are emitted to the audit log stream and delivered to your logging endpoint. We timestamp, include actor identity (SSO subject), and correlate with request ids.
[00:06:06] Marcus: Network security controls - can you run the inference containers in isolated subnets, private ENIs, and restrict SGs so only the internal LB and the management host can reach them?
[00:06:14] Daniel: Absolutely. Inference nodes are just compute nodes in your subnets. Security groups and NACLs control reachability. We recommend a pattern: control plane subnet (management) and compute subnet (inference) with no inbound from internet. The internal NLB in front of inference nodes is only accessible from your app subnets or via PrivateLink.
[00:06:33] Alex: Do you support mTLS between internal components?
[00:06:36] Daniel: Yes. We can enable mTLS for intra-cluster traffic. Mutual TLS with certs issued by your CA or a Redwood-managed PKI - for maximum control use your CA and rotate certs via your tooling.
[00:06:47] Priya: Any dependency on ephemeral external DNS we should worry about?
[00:06:51] Daniel: We support split-horizon DNS. You can host internal records for service discovery; no external DNS required. We'll provide example Route 53 private hosted zone or similar for other clouds.
[00:07:02] Maya: On firewalling - you can implement restrictive outbound rules, and we will not attempt to circumvent them. The only connections Redwood needs are to your logging endpoints, KMS endpoints (if using cloud KMS), and optionally a control plane health endpoint if you choose managed control plane.
[00:07:17] Ellen: If we lock down egress to only KMS endpoints for key ops, will the runtime still function?
[00:07:21] Daniel: Yes. You need to allow the KMS endpoints and endpoints for any S3 buckets you're using for model artifacts. If you host model artifacts in your account, no traffic leaves your account.
[00:07:31] Alex: Model updates - if we want to pull curated weights from Redwood, how is that delivered?
[00:07:36] Daniel: We support model bundles delivered as signed artifacts. You can pull them from a presigned S3 URL or we can upload into your bucket via a secure transfer with an approved role. All transfers are signed and verifiable.
[00:07:49] Priya: What about threat detection - do you emit events for anomalous requests or rate spikes?
[00:07:54] Daniel: We emit telemetry - request rates, latencies, error spikes - to your metrics endpoint. For content-based anomalies you can plug into our moderation hooks; we'll forward flagged events to your SIEM.
[00:08:04] Marcus: Any recommendations for network ACLs vs security groups?
[00:08:08] Daniel: SGs for instance-level allow-lists, NACLs for subnet-level stateless rules. Use SGs for fine-grained control between pods/instances; NACLs as a guardrail. We'll include sample SG + NACL configs in the diagram.
[00:08:20] Alex: Let's talk about failover - if a region goes down, does Redwood attempt cross-region fallback and does that violate data residency?
[00:08:28] Maya: We have routing policies adjustable by you. For strict data residency you can disable cross-region fallback. By default we prefer local region and only failover to same-country region variants if allowed. We'll surface those controls in the console and in the deployment manifest.
[00:08:43] Priya: Encryption-in-transit: TLS 1.3, perfect forward secrecy?
[00:08:46] Daniel: Yes, TLS 1.3 with PFS. For intra-cluster mTLS, we use mutual TLS with strong ciphers.
[00:08:54] Ellen: Can we get logs ingested into our existing Splunk instance?
[00:08:58] Daniel: Absolutely. We support Splunk HEC, syslog, CloudWatch, GCP Logging, and forwarders. We'll provide a sample Splunk HEC config.
[00:09:07] Alex: Any blockers for us running this in our highest-security environment?
[00:09:11] Daniel: The main items are ensuring KMS access, private endpoints for artifact retrieval, and egress rules for logging/KMS. If you require HSM-only key operations and no service-to-service calls to public endpoints, we can support a fully on-prem HSM flow but that will be the longest path for onboarding.
[00:09:28] Priya: What about penetration testing and attestation?
[00:09:31] Maya: We can provide our third-party pen test reports for the hosted control plane. For Private deployments, we recommend a scoping test with your red team in a staging environment; we can support that and help run a joint pentest.
[00:09:44] Marcus: For the POC, we want to run a small workload with tokenized data and test latencies. We'll need a checklist of required IAM roles and networking steps.
[00:09:53] Daniel: We'll provide a POC checklist: VPC/subnets, route tables, security groups, NAT/Egress proxy, S3 buckets and roles, KMS grants, and an IAM role for Redwood's operator with minimal privileges.
[00:10:05] Ellen: Can you summarize the shared responsibility?
[00:10:08] Maya: Sure - Redwood is responsible for runtime code, patches, and controls internal to the container OS and service. You're responsible for VPC, network controls, IAM, key policies, and storage retention. We'll share a formal matrix.
[00:10:21] Alex: Ok let's open it up for questions.
[00:10:25] Priya: One last detailed ask: we require HSM-backed key wrapping for model encryption keys and want to rotate every 90 days. Is rotation supported without downtime?
[00:10:34] Daniel: Yes. We support key rotation workflows using KMS key aliases and key grants; rotation is seamless if you perform a re-encrypt-in-place pattern and revoke old grants after rollover. We'll share the recommended rotation steps.
[00:10:47] Marcus: On firewalling, what about egress to telemetry endpoints - is there built-in batching to reduce calls?
[00:10:53] Daniel: We batch metrics and logs and support push to your batching endpoint. You can further front it with a local agent to buffer and apply DLP before forwarding.
[00:11:04] Alex: Any outstanding compliance caveats?
[00:11:06] Maya: The only caveat is for fully air-gapped on-prem installs we need to scope model delivery and licensing. For cloud VPCs, everything stated is supported.
[00:11:16] Ellen: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[00:11:19] Maya: Recap: we will send SOC2 + whitepaper, Daniel will send VPC diagram + POC checklist, we'll schedule a POC in your dev account, and Marcus will provision access.
[00:11:30] Alex: That works. Thanks everyone.
[00:11:33] Maya: Thanks - we'll follow up with links. End of call.

Notes on transcription: occasional minor mis-transcribes (e.g., "Redwood Private" sometimes referenced as "Redwood Privet"), some speaker labels simplified. Links shared during call: /link/security-whitepaper.pdf (placeholder), /link/soc2-redwood-2025.pdf, /link/poc-checklist.xlsx.
